h: Gyanesh Kumar will not go: the last window to save democracy
dek: Ajaz Ashraf argues that there is little hope of Gyanesh Kumar resigning, and if the opposition does not build pressure both on the street and in the Supreme Court before the UP election, the last chance to save the Election Commission's image will slip away too.
body: On 23 October, between 500 and 700 people gathered at Delhi's Gol Dak Khana. Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das of the Cockroach Janata Party said in a video that 'Gyanu will have to go'. Ajaz Ashraf asked: what happens if Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar does not resign? His answer is that resignation is unlikely, because the government's majority in the Lok Sabha means an impeachment motion cannot pass, and the Supreme Court has long avoided upsetting the government.

The BJP will not let him go, because that would mean the lists were tampered with to win elections. The writer compares this to the 2021 farmers' movement, when the government withdrew the laws before the UP election. For now the protest is small. A woman constable said her heart is not in this duty, that this government is against 'We, the People of India', and that the government is afraid only of farmers and students.

The real tangle is the opposition's. If it wins UP, the BJP will say there was nothing wrong with the system; if it loses, merely contesting the election will legitimise the system. The writer asked analysts whether the election should have been boycotted until Gyanesh Kumar goes. All of them called it impractical, because parties exist for power and a boycott works only when turnout is very low.

According to the writer, the blow of SIR (Special Intensive Revision) falls hardest in the cities, and the debate over it is louder in cities than in villages, while anger over livelihoods and education is far wider. His conclusion is that only two months remain before the UP election is notified in January. If the BJP wins UP, even the hope of restoring faith in the election system will break.
nazar: This article reminds us that institutions do not mend themselves. When the Election Commission is the one that must answer and the Supreme Court too does not want to clash with the government, pressure will have to come from the street. And that pressure is incomplete without the voices of those whose names were cut: Muslims, Dalits, Adivasis (indigenous communities), workers, farmers and women.
The woman constable is the article's biggest source of hope. Not every state employee is a tool of power, and whenever people inside begin to speak the truth, the fear of power weakens.
sawal: If Gyanesh Kumar does not go, whose pressure will work?
ref: Impeachment
The process under the Constitution for removing the President, the Chief Election Commissioner and others from office, which needs a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision, a fresh scrutiny of the voter lists. The charge is that a large number of genuine voters were struck off in it.
ank: Until the UP election is notified
photo_note: Symbolic image: a protest at Jantar Mantar

h: 124 officers to the rescue: a trick to dodge accountability
dek: Avay Shukla's tone is sharp: the open letter from 124 former officers defending Gyanesh Kumar and SIR is a document for dodging accountability, and the Election Commission's own rollbacks are witness to it.
body: An open letter from 124 former officers has appeared in defence of Gyanesh Kumar and SIR. Avay Shukla calls it a document for dodging accountability. According to him, some of the signatories have faced corruption charges, some have been close to the ruling side, and one had himself admitted that he issued orders under political pressure.

According to the writer, the letter is not an impartial opinion but praise of power. It praises the Election Commission's past work, calls SIR necessary, and corners those demanding Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. Shukla says the same commission has reversed several of its decisions in the past few weeks, which is proof that the protest's charges were not empty.

He lists them: the controversial declaration on Form 6 was removed, officials' access to ECINet was restored, a committee was set up to examine the software, the commission acknowledged the letter from both election commissioners, limits were placed on Form 7, and a drive began in 17 states to add voters who had been left out. According to the writer, the commission also conceded that it has no list of Amit Shah's 'infiltrators'.

Shukla reads this as a quiet confession by the commission. According to him, after 13 crore (130 million) names were struck off, this stance strengthens the belief that SIR was carried out to win the Bengal and Bihar elections. He says defending such a letter is not a free opinion but support for authoritarianism, and the question is what answer these officers will give the public.
nazar: The letter from 124 former officers shows that a large part of the bureaucracy still wants to save its image by kneeling before power. This is not just about Gyanesh Kumar, it is a question about the fairness of the entire administrative system.
Those whose names were cut have no access to officers. In such a situation, even the silence of honest officers works against them.
sawal: Does the officers' letter save the truth, or power?
ref: Constitutional Conduct Group
A group of former officers that has spoken out openly against government decisions on the Constitution and citizens' rights.
Form 7
The objection form used to remove a name from the voter list, which was used on a large scale in SIR.
photo_note: Symbolic image: Parliament House, New Delhi

h: A witchcraft plot: the new trick to bury the question of vote theft
dek: Rajendra Sharma's satire: as the demand for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation grows, the government wants to build a witchcraft conspiracy and push the real question, vote theft, to the side.
body: Rajendra Sharma's satire opens at an imaginary emergency meeting, where the government is describing the demand for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation and the protests as a foreign conspiracy. The meeting discusses imposing an Emergency, because the government feels the protest is growing and every weapon can be tried to stop it.

The home minister reveals a 'conspiracy' in Doharighat, Mau. A photograph of the prime minister was found near a cremation ground, with coconuts tied with kalava (sacred thread) at its four corners and lemons pierced with needles placed below. The police have registered a case of a plot to murder through witchcraft and handed the inquiry to the NIA.

The defence minister suggests that the plot must have a thread leading to Pakistan, so Operation Sindoor-2 should be launched. The prime minister says he will not impose an Emergency, but the witchcraft plot can be linked to those demanding Gyanesh's resignation and they can be accused of a murder plot.

The edge of the satire is that the government can go to any length to distract from the questions of vote theft and SIR. The more absurd the plot, the less room is left for the real question. And when there is no answer, only the story of a plot remains. The writer also shows that godhi media (lapdog media) helps turn this drama into a serious debate.
nazar: The satire here is not there just to make you laugh. It shows that the government can make any absurd story serious to avoid the real question, and a section of the media gives it wind.
The real cost of the joke is paid by the poor and those on the margins. When the debate moves to witchcraft, the workers, farmers and minorities pushed out of the vote are left behind once again.
sawal: Is witchcraft the real issue, or a trick to distract?
ref: NIA
The National Investigation Agency, which investigates cases linked to terrorism and the country's security.
Operation Sindoor
India's military action against Pakistan in May 2025, a name the government itself gave it.
photo_note: Symbolic image: police barricade

h: A rattled government: stick for the Cockroach, softness for the big parties
dek: Anand Mishra reads it this way: the government wants to crush the young people of the Cockroach Janata Party with jail and restrictions, while giving the Congress and other big parties some room on the street.
body: Abhijeet Deepke of the Cockroach Janata Party got bail with surety on 17 October, while Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were sent to five days of judicial custody on 14 October and released on 21 October. They had been arrested for protesting the removal of Jantar Mantar from the list of designated protest sites. A magistrate stepped aside from the hearing, citing a threat to his life, and the release was delayed.

According to the writer, the government had all but shut Delhi down on 10 October. 57 metro stations stayed closed, several trains were cancelled and more than 400 people were taken into custody. The Supreme Court said a hammer should not be used to kill a fly. After that, the INDIA bloc held a march on 12 October and announced a Ramlila rally for 1 November.

Not everyone in the protest is the same. The BJD came onto the street after several years, while the DMK stayed away. The AAP did not join at first and later sent representatives. Kerala passed a resolution seeking the removal of the commission, more than a hundred people were taken into custody in Bengaluru, and Andhra, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry kept their distance. Mamata Banerjee used the platform to rebuild her own politics.
The writer's conclusion is that this double strategy is plain to see. The government is using an iron hand on the Cockroach Janata Party, while giving some room to big parties like the Congress.
nazar: Beating the youngest and most restless section while giving big parties room on the street is an old trick. It is an attempt to blunt the edge of the movement, but it also shows whom the government sees as its real threat.
The students who have no lawyers, media or money are the ones who must fight the longest legal battle. That inequality is also the movement's biggest weakness.
sawal: Why the stick only for the young, and softness for the big parties?
ref: Peace bond
A written condition and surety that a person will keep the peace in future, which the police often impose on protesters.
Jantar Mantar
The road beside the 18th-century observatory near Parliament, which has been the country's best-known protest site since the 1990s.
photo_note: Symbolic image: students' protest march

h: From Shaheen Bagh to Jantar Mantar: women are the movement's new voice
dek: Qutubuddin Shahid writes that the leadership of female students and young women in Delhi's protests should be seen not as a victory for any one party but as part of a long social change.
body: In Delhi's recent protests, the presence of girls and female students stood out most. Qutubuddin Shahid writes that this is not a victory for any one party or organisation but a sign of a long social change. Faces like Neha Bora, Ratna Singh, Umm Habiba and Gurmehar Kaur became the mark of that change.

According to the writer, the government has had its eye on students from the start, especially those at JNU, Jamia, Aligarh Muslim University, Allahabad University and BHU who kept asking questions. He says the police were harsher towards the boys, so the female students took the lead. The long imprisonment of Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam kept deepening that fear.

In early October, women journalists at Delhi's protests accused the police of sexual abuse. The writer says these allegations need an independent inquiry, because videos surfaced along with the charges and it is not right to ignore them.

The thread connects to Shaheen Bagh, where women led the protest against the citizenship law. That was when the belief broke that Muslim women want to stay within the home. Now a new generation is on the street over exam transparency, jobs, the right to vote and the accountability of institutions.

The writer remembers Aruna Asaf Ali, Sarojini Naidu, Kasturba Gandhi, Bhikaiji Cama, Lakshmi Sahgal, B. Amma and Usha Mehta. He says this movement is not a thing of one moment but the beginning of a bigger change.
nazar: Women coming onto the street is a change not only in the movement but in society. When female students and young women lead, the family, the university and the government all have to listen to them.
But this change will last only if safety and equality are not just slogans. An inquiry into the women journalists' allegations and the participation of women on the margins are both necessary.
sawal: Will women's leadership last, or is it just the shine of a moment?
ref: Shaheen Bagh
A neighbourhood in Delhi where women held a sit-in for months in 2019-20 against the citizenship amendment law.
AISA
The All India Students' Association, a left-wing student organisation whose president, Neha Bora, became a major face of this movement.
photo_note: Collage: Deshkaal

h: The foreign hand refrain: this suspicion will cost India dearly
dek: Raja Karthikeya argues that crying foreign conspiracy without evidence not only smears the protest but also damages India's diplomatic capital and the credibility of its election technology.
body: Raja Karthikeya writes that foreign embassies in Delhi have suddenly become more interested, because the impact of SIR is not limited to Indian politics. India's voter base is 95 crore (950 million), and in January 2026 the Election Commission presented ECINet to representatives of 42 countries and 27 embassies.

According to the writer, a Pacific country was discussing adopting ECINet, but questions about the centralisation of the lists and the large-scale removal of names in the name of 'logical discrepancy' have reduced its confidence. This also damages the image of India's digital public infrastructure.

He mentions the 6 October issue of 'Organiser', which alleged that funding for the Cockroach Janata Party came from America, passed through ISIS, ISI, Riyadh and criminals in Mumbai and Delhi, and reached the movement. The basis was a social media video of a masked man. The BJP president alleged on 10 October that the opposition was working for foreign forces.

The writer says that if there is evidence, India should take firm action, but diplomacy does not run on speeches alone. India has signed, or is signing, trade deals with the US, Britain, Australia and the European Union, and next year there is an election to the UN Security Council. Such allegations harm India's interests.
His conclusion is that if the image of democracy is to be kept, the noise about a foreign conspiracy must stop. Strategic autonomy is necessary, but calling every protest a foreign hand is dangerous.
nazar: The cry of the 'foreign hand' has been raised against every movement that asks power for answers. It leaves the real issue, the names cut from the voter list, behind.
The diplomatic damage is not the government's alone. Students studying abroad, exporters, workers and minorities all pay the price of this suspicion.
sawal: How can every protest be a foreign conspiracy?
ref: ECINet
The Election Commission's centralised digital platform, used to link voter lists and remove names.
Strategic autonomy
The freedom to take decisions in foreign policy in the national interest, without coming under the pressure of a big power.
photo_note: Symbolic image: Parliament House

h: Bangladesh ahead of India: so why the fear of infiltration?
dek: Shoaib Daniyal argues that once Bangladesh's per capita income is above India's, the cry of infiltration sounds pointless, and it makes clear that the real target of SIR is Muslim citizens.
body: Shoaib Daniyal writes that SIR has so far removed 13 crore (130 million) voters from the draft lists. There were big protests against it in Delhi, thousands of people were taken into custody and dozens of journalists were also picked up. Critics allege that it targets Muslims most, since they generally do not vote for the BJP.

The government's argument is that SIR is meant to catch infiltrators who came from Bangladesh. Amit Shah said the Congress was protecting infiltrators. But according to the writer, the Election Commission has no record of how many infiltrators were caught in SIR, while there is already evidence of thousands of genuine Indians having their names cut.

The International Monetary Fund said that in financial year 2026, Bangladesh's per capita GDP is slightly higher than India's. People generally migrate from a poorer country to a richer one, so it is strange for a country like India to fear this. The same happened with the 2019 Assam NRC: Bangladesh was one and a half times richer than Assam, yet BJP leaders were claiming 60 lakh (6 million) infiltrators, while 19 lakh (1.9 million) names were cut in the NRC and most of them were Hindus.

The writer asks: if crores of Bangladeshis are living in India, why are cases not being filed against them? His answer is that the cry of infiltration is only a device to distract, and the real target is Muslim citizens. Across the country, Muslim names have been cut at a higher rate, and the BJP gains directly from this.

His conclusion is that the Bangladesh story has neither evidence nor economic logic, but this big lie is shaking the foundation of democracy. He says this big lie is shaking the foundation of the right to vote.
nazar: The per capita income argument about Bangladesh is not just a statistic, it is a mirror. It shows that the cry of infiltration was always based on fear, never on evidence.

Those whose names were cut are often Muslims, the poor, workers and women. For them this debate is a question of life and death, so the opposition must put their citizenship at the centre, not just election arithmetic.
sawal: If there is no infiltration, why are names being cut?
ref: NRC
The National Register of Citizens, the citizenship check carried out in Assam in 2019, in which hundreds of thousands of people were left off the list.
Per capita GDP
The average reached by dividing a country's total income by its population, which gives a rough idea of the standard of living.

h: Europe at dusk: the crisis is not from outside, it is in its own model
dek: The promise of European integration is breaking and the right is rising from within that same project, argues V. V. P. Sharma.
body: For the past three decades, Europe has assumed that economic integration, a shared currency, liberal democracy and the free movement of people would slowly end the continent's old national enmities. The European Union was seen not just as a market but as proof that institutions, prosperity and shared values can heal the old wounds of history. V. V. P. Sharma says that faith is now breaking.

According to him, Europe's trouble is not only external. The system that promised prosperity left industrial towns insecure, many families were left behind, and people began to feel that Brussels was far from their everyday worries. So the right and nationalism cannot be called simply an attack from outside. They are a contradiction born within the same project.

Sharma takes up Hegel's idea that philosophy takes flight at dusk and opens the argument from there. A civilisation understands the meaning of its own arrangements only when its way of life begins to tire. Europe is at that turn today, having to see what contradictions the promise of integration gave birth to.

The essay also takes up the question of growing dependence on America. Europe has left much of its security, economic policy and strategic imagination to Washington. The question is how much a political community can claim sovereignty when its security and economic direction are decided elsewhere.

Sharma does not say Europe is finished. Hegel's owl does not announce the death of a civilisation; it records the moment when a system, moving towards its end, begins to become intelligible. The question is not whom to blame, but how Europe's own decisions and institutions together produce the crisis.
nazar: For India, Europe's experience is not just foreign news. Here too, amid fast growth, many regions and workers have been left behind, and when governments speak only of markets and institutions, anger turns towards those who are weakest.

Like Europe, India has to protect its strategic freedom and its federal, multilingual society at the same time. If integration does not come with a reckoning of who is left out, minorities, Dalits, Adivasis and workers are the first to be targeted.
sawal: When will Europe own up to the contradictions of its own project?
ref: Hegel's owl
The German philosopher Hegel's image of philosophy taking flight at dusk. It means that an age reveals its meaning only when it is moving towards its end.
Strategic autonomy
A country's capacity to take decisions on security, trade and foreign policy by looking at its own interest, not under pressure from big powers.

h: In France the question is not 'riots' but broken schools
dek: Rokhaya Diallo says the government is hiding behind images of violence to escape the students' poverty and their demand for education.
body: Images from the student movement that has run in France since September reached around the world: broken windows, looting and fire. Rokhaya Diallo writes that condemning violence is fair, but the government turned these images into its own defence. By calling the whole movement a riot, it escaped the question students had been raising for years.

The essay keeps a tally of police action. Fourteen-year-old Eden's jaw was broken and teeth knocked out, sixteen-year-old Maël lost the sight in one eye, fifteen-year-old Evan's hand was blown off by a stun grenade. By 14 October, 7,950 people had been taken into custody after the movement began, 85 per cent of them minors. After 17 October, 2,700 more people were picked up.

The violence is not only on the street. In France, 9.8 million people live below the poverty line, the most since the 1990s. 53 billionaires hold nearly as much wealth as half the population. The state of the schools is plain proof: one school in Mayotte packs 2,300 children into space meant for 900, water drips from ceilings in the Paris suburbs, and windows will not open in 40-degree heat.

In 2024-25, 2.02 crore (20.2 million) teaching hours were not taught in state secondary schools, that is one in every ten. Of these, 1.5 crore (15 million) hours were wasted simply because no one was put in place of absent teachers. Spending per student has fallen by 20 per cent since 2017.

Macron deployed 70,000 police officers, spoke of banning the movement and accused his opponents of plotting to bring down the republic. The prime minister told the opposition it must choose between a republic run by the police and the agenda of rioters. Diallo says the government is waiting for the movement to tire, but if broken schools and poverty are not ended, a new movement will rise again.
nazar: The riot the French government talks about is really a way of smearing young people's anger. In India too, students' anger over state schools, teacher shortages and rising fees is constantly ignored, and the police reach those who protest first.
If governments speak only of law and order instead of schools, jobs and poverty, the trust of minority, Dalit and working-class families breaks. That is the lesson from France.
sawal: If the schools are broken, why talk only of riots?
ref: Custody
Under French law, the police can hold a person for a limited time without charge being framed. Thousands of people went through this process during the movement, most of them minors.
Banlieue
The outer areas of France's big cities, where working-class and immigrant families live. The shortage of state schools and services shows there most of all.

h: Brazil: Lula's return, a turning point in South America
dek: Guillaume Long argues that Brazil's election checked both the right-wing wave and Trump's pressure.
body: In Brazil, 80-year-old Lula fell short of an outright win in the first round, taking 47 per cent against Flávio Bolsonaro's 45 per cent. Then, after three weeks of intense campaigning, he won the second round with 51.8 per cent to Bolsonaro's 48.2 per cent. Guillaume Long writes that this is not just a victory for Brazil but a blow to the right-wing wave across Latin America.

Lula's economic record was not weak. Between 2023 and 2025, Brazil's economy grew 9.2 per cent, while the average growth of its South American neighbours was 5.6 per cent. Unemployment came down from 9.3 per cent in 2022 to 5.4 per cent in 2026. The country moved off the United Nations hunger list in 2025, and deforestation in the Amazon fell to its lowest in decades.

Yet there was discontent. Millions of people were stuck in credit card debt, interest rates were very high and online gambling was eating into family incomes. Lula answered with promises of debt relief, a ban on online betting, social benefits, fuel subsidies and a five-day week instead of six.

Bolsonaro chose the path of cuts, privatisation, tax reductions and tough action on crime. He spoke of building five maximum-security prisons like El Salvador's and of using lethal force against armed criminals. His agenda also included a promise to pardon his father, sentenced to 27 years and to give relief to those convicted for the 8 January 2023 attack.

According to Long, this election was also about sovereignty. Trump imposed tariffs, sanctioned a Supreme Court judge and openly backed Flávio. Two days after meeting Flávio in the Oval Office in May, Brazil's two biggest criminal organisations were declared foreign terrorist organisations, which could open the way for US military action.
nazar: Lula's victory is a reminder that anger born of inequality and debt can bring back the left, not only the right. In India too, farmers, workers and small traders are troubled by rising prices and debt, and governments often give them only election speeches.
In the face of Trump's pressure and tariffs, Brazil spoke of sovereignty. India too must put its independence, and the interests of farmers and workers, first in trade and defence deals with America.
sawal: Is the right-wing wave really slowing?
ref: Second round
In Brazil's presidential election, if no one gets more than half the votes in the first round, the top two candidates face another vote. This is called the runoff or second round.
Donroe Doctrine

A term used in the essay for Trump's Latin America policy, a new version of the old Monroe Doctrine. It means that America claims the right to military and political intervention in its neighbourhood.

h: Climate displacement: people leaving home, whose bill is it?
dek: Farah Kabir says help for Bangladesh's displaced must come as grants, not as a debt trap.
body: According to a 2026 Asian Development Bank report, by 2050, 1.33 crore (13.3 million) people in Bangladesh could be displaced inside their own country because of climate change. Rising seas, water shortages and falling farm yields are given as the reasons. Farah Kabir says that no one is there to pay the bill for those who will lose home, land and livelihood.

Between 2014 and 2023, disasters displaced people in Bangladesh 1.47 crore (14.7 million) times. That is not the number of different people but the number of displacement events. In an assessment by the International Organization for Migration and the government, about 50 lakh (5 million) people were found to be displaced inside the country by disasters in 2025, and 63 per cent of them had already been uprooted before April 2020.

Displacement does not take only a home. Land, earnings, savings, schools, hospitals and the web of relationships are all taken away. Women lose their claim to property and compensation, and unpaid work at home grows heavier on them. For the disabled, the elderly and communities on the margins, both help and infrastructure become scarce.

People do not sit idle. They find other ways to earn, borrow, sell their things, go for seasonal work. But once savings run out, this too breaks. Kabir says Bangladesh has frameworks like a national strategy on internal displacement, a 2022-2042 action plan, a climate adaptation plan and Delta Plan 2100, but the question is whether money and decisions reach the ground.

Her demand is that at COP31, rich countries keep their promises on cuts and give climate finance as grants, not as a debt trap. The money should be in the hands of local communities, spent on reducing risk, permanent homes, water, livelihoods and early warning systems. The countries that have emitted the least should not have to pay the highest price.
nazar: India must ask the same question. Farmers, fisherfolk and Adivasis in Assam, the Sundarbans, Odisha and Bihar are uprooted by floods and drought every year, but their voice is weak in the debate on climate finance.

Governments make big promises at conferences, but when people leave home they get no compensation, no work in the cities and no place to live. Climate justice means exactly this: that the weakest get help first.
sawal: Who will pay compensation when people leave home?
ref: COP31
The 31st United Nations conference on climate change is called COP31. There, countries discuss cutting emissions, climate finance and help for displaced people.
Loss and Damage Fund
An international fund set up to cover damage from climate disasters that cannot be prevented by cuts or adaptation. It should not be limited to relief after a disaster.
photo_note: Symbolic image: flood and erosion

h: America's midterms: Trump's standing and the war on Iran
dek: Aakar Patel asks whether, on 3 November, American voters will put their wallets and their anger over the war above party loyalty.
body: America holds its midterm elections on 3 November. They fall in the middle of the president's four-year term, which is why they are called midterms. Members of Congress face the voters every two years. If Trump's Republican Party loses control of one or both chambers, it will be harder for him to pass laws, get judges appointed and have officials confirmed, and the opposition will be able to open investigations.

The writer says the election will tell us something about human nature. Democracy assumes that people vote by reason, not like a tribe. But Trump's approval rating is below 40 per cent, and his numbers on the economy are worse. Fuel has become expensive since the war on Iran began in February, inflation has risen and so have interest rates on home loans. The tariff war has added fuel to the fire.

Since his party controls both chambers of Congress and has a conservative majority on the Supreme Court, voters who feel let down have no one else to blame but Trump. He has endorsed sitting candidates against rivals from his own party, so a vote for them is a vote for him and his policies.

The second big question is Israel. Israel's popularity in America has fallen sharply, and Democratic candidates are openly critical. The writer links this to Zohran Mamdani's campaign, which won while supporting Palestinians. AIPAC, the lobby group, has been so discredited that it has stopped endorsing candidates. The question is whether the Democrats, if they win, can end the unconditional support Israel has long enjoyed.

The third reason matters to us too. Because of the war, oil has gone above $115 a barrel, against $60 before the fighting. That directly affects the crores of Indians in the Gulf and their families here. The writer believes a Republican defeat would weaken support for the war on Iran. The short two-year term gives voters a chance to correct the government's course, and this time many hope they will use it.
nazar: American elections look distant from India, but they bear directly on our wallets and on the people who work in the Gulf. Oil prices, remittances and the war on Iran are links in the same chain.
If American voters choose party loyalty despite the pain in their wallets, that will not be just America's story. It will show how weak the hope of reasoned voting has become in democracies.
sawal: Will the pain in the wallet beat party loyalty?
ref: Midterms
US elections held in the middle of a president's term, when members of Congress face the voters.
AIPAC
The pro-Israel lobby in the US that has long endorsed and funded candidates.

h: In Punjab, the compulsion to go it alone and the debate over an Akali tie-up
dek: Jagdeep Singh Sindhu argues that the BJP's own hold in Punjab is limited, which makes an alliance with the Akali Dal a necessity, but seat-sharing will decide on whose terms it happens.
body: Amit Shah's statement about forming an NDA government in Punjab has revived talk of an alliance. Yet the state BJP president, Kewal Singh Dhillon, and other leaders have kept claiming that the party will contest all 117 seats alone. The party's 'drug-free Punjab' march also drew less support than expected.

The writer says the limits of fighting alone are clear. Despite a higher vote share in the 2024 Lok Sabha election, the BJP could not score any big win in the municipal polls. In assembly-segment terms, the BJP led in 23 and the Akali Dal in nine, and their combined share was about 32 per cent. On that basis, a lead in 57 seats is projected, but Lok Sabha numbers do not decide an assembly result.

The BJP's traditional base is urban. It has tried to embrace Sikh religious and social symbols, but has not built acceptance across the state. The Akali Dal's strength lies in rural areas, Sikh institutions and the politics of regional identity. An alliance can join their geographical and social reach, but there is no guarantee that votes will transfer fully.

The real test will be seat-sharing. If the BJP offers the Akali Dal enough seats and a respectable role in the leadership, it will show its electoral compulsion. If it insists on contesting all 117 seats and demands a big share, it will be clear that the BJP wants to build an independent identity rather than stay junior to its old ally.

The BJP's biggest aim is to keep the Congress out. The Congress has gained new life under its new president, Partap Singh, and that worries the BJP. The influence of the Waris Punjab De and the factions that broke away from the Akali Dal has not spread across the state either. So the BJP wants an alliance to do several things at once: form a government, expand its own base and limit the Akali Dal's role. For the Akali Dal too, going alone is not easy, with a limited base and a weak showing in 2022.
nazar: In Punjab, an alliance is not just arithmetic of seats but a bargain over identity. For the BJP, going with the Akali Dal means a route to Sikh voters; for the Akali Dal, it means a relationship with power in Delhi.

The article itself admits that the BJP cannot break the state's anger over drugs and farming on its own. The question is whether this alliance is the return of an old partnership or a pretence covering the weakness of both parties.
sawal: On whose terms will the alliance be sealed? The seats will tell.
ref: Shiromani Akali Dal
Punjab's old Sikh-centred party, a BJP ally for decades until they parted ways in 2020.
Waris Punjab De
An organisation linked to Amritpal Singh that speaks of a separate Sikh politics in Punjab.
photo_note: Symbolic image: women working in a field

h: Manipur journalist charged under NSA, acquitted after eight years
dek: The journalist was held under the NSA for four and a half months over social media posts criticising Biren Singh. He is now going to court for compensation and accountability.
body: Kishorchandra Wangkhemcha, a journalist from Manipur, was dragged into charges of sedition, obscenity and defamation eight years ago over social media posts criticising the then chief minister Biren Singh. In April this year, the state's chief judicial magistrate acquitted him. On Monday, at the Press Club of India in Delhi, he said he will now claim compensation from four people.

These four are Nongthombam Nimbus, acting president of the BJP state unit, Pangambam Premananda, then general secretary, and the two investigating officers, Konthoujam Bobby and Toijam Amalkumar. The case was filed on a private complaint by BJP leaders, which the police later took up on their own. In connection with this, Wangkhemcha was kept in detention for four and a half months under the National Security Act, or NSA.

In its ruling, the court said the case was tainted from the start and the investigation was full of prejudice against the accused. It also emerged that the sedition section was used in a case whose charge sheet did not even mention sedition. The journalist's lawyer, Emmanuel, said the government had wanted to silence him from the beginning.

The dispute had its roots in a comment about celebrating Rani Jhansi's birthday, in which he called it an insult to Manipur's freedom fighters. Wangkhemcha said a lack of food in jail gave him diabetes. He wants the case not to stay limited to Manipur but to become an example for the future.
nazar: This is not just one journalist's victory. It is a question about the way people from small communities who criticise the state are silenced with weapons like sedition and the National Security Act. Doing journalism in Manipur is already hard, and when a case runs for eight years, the effect of fear does not fall on one person alone.
sawal: After paying the price for criticism, who will now fix accountability?
ref: NSA
The National Security Act, 1980, under which a person can be held for months without trial.
photo_note: Symbolic image: a newspaper printing press

h: No prosecution for filing Form 6: Supreme Court
dek: After voters were struck off the rolls in Maharashtra, the Supreme Court assured those filing Form 6 that they will not be prosecuted.
body: The Supreme Court said orally on Monday that people who file Form 6 after being removed from the voters' list during the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, will not face prosecution. The court was hearing a petition challenging the revision of Maharashtra's voters' list.

The petitioner's lawyer said that if already registered voters file Form 6 describing themselves as new voters, it is an offence. Chief Justice Surya Kant replied, "Do not worry, no one will be prosecuted." The court issued notice to the Election Commission but refused to extend the deadline for claims and objections or to hold back the final voters' list.

The petition said that of Maharashtra's nearly nine crore voters, about three crore names were removed after the draft list. In Mumbai and Pune, redevelopment of buildings led to about 40 per cent of residents being marked absent and their names being cut. Mumbai has 3,500 such projects and Pune 1,500.

The court fixed the next hearing for 5 November. Earlier, the Delhi High Court had said that the fear of prosecution for filing Form 6 is baseless, because the instruction came from the Election Commission itself. Former chief election commissioner SY Quraishi had said that voters whose names were cut cannot file Form 6.
nazar: Being struck off the voters' list is not a technical glitch. When people displaced from their homes by redevelopment, tenants and labourers drop off the list, the door of democracy closes on them. The court's assurance is necessary, but the real question is who will fix the mistake of names being cut.
sawal: When will a voter whose name was cut get the right to vote again?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision, the Election Commission process in which the voters' list is checked house by house.
Form 6
The form for registering a new voter, in which a person has to declare that they have never been registered before.
photo_note: Supreme Court building, New Delhi

h: Christian families attacked in West Medinipur, no arrests
dek: Three Christian families in Patlapur village allege they were beaten for three days, their clothes torn and Durga Puja rituals forced on them. Thirteen people are named in the FIR.
body: In Patlapur village in West Bengal's West Medinipur district, three Christian families have alleged that they were beaten, threatened and forced to change their religion for three straight days from 18 to 20 October. The families identified the attackers as members of the Bajrang Dal. The FIR registered in the Chandrakona police station area names 13 people, but no arrests have been made so far.

Laxmi Mondal, one of the women, said the threats grew sharper on 16 October and the beating began two days later. According to her, Ranjit Dolui struck her below the ear and she fell unconscious. When she came to, she felt people pulling at her sari and tearing her blouse. The allegation is that the attackers poured water on her face and, raising "Jai Shri Ram" slogans, said she had been purified.

The families allege that on 19 October they were forcibly taken to a Durga Puja pandal in Dangal and made to offer anjali. They said that on 20 October the men were taken to a separate place and threatened with death. Out of fear, three minor girls were sent to relatives' homes. A police post was set up only after the FIR.

Papai Sultana, superintendent of police of West Medinipur, said the FIR has been registered and the families will be given protection. According to a local teacher, no such incident had happened in the village for decades. The victims said, who will protect us after the police leave?
nazar: Punishing people by treating conversion as a crime is not new, but the failure to arrest those who carried it out is a big question. This incident reflects the fear that arose over the safety of minority families in Bengal after the change of power. The humiliation of the women is not one family's matter; it is a question of the whole community's trust.
sawal: Who will protect the families after the police leave?
ref: Anjali
The prayer offered with folded hands before the goddess during Durga Puja, which was forced on the families here.
photo_note: Symbolic image: a village in Assam

h: Candles lit for Sahil Wakode, police pick up 140
dek: Mumbai Police detained students and activists gathered at Chaityabhoomi in memory of Sahil Wakode; the same day about 120 Adivasi students were also picked up from Shivaji Park.
body: Mumbai Police on Sunday detained around 140 students and activists during two separate protests in the Dadar area. Among them were stand-up comedian Masoom Rajwani and several Ambedkarite activists who had gathered at Chaityabhoomi to demand accountability for the death of Sahil Wakode, a 22-year-old Dalit student at IIT Bombay.

Wakode was found dead in his hostel room on 18 September. His parents and fellow students have alleged caste-based harassment. The complaint names Professor Suryanarayan Dula and invokes the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act along with charges of abetment of suicide. Dula and the institute's director, Shireesh Kedare, deny the allegations.

Protesters alleged that the police picked people up twice, around six and seven in the evening, including those standing with candles or placards. One participant said they were put in a van without being told why. Those detained were later released from the Tardeo, Worli and Dadar police stations.

Of these, about 120 Adivasi students and activists were detained at Shivaji Park. They were seeking answers from Maharashtra's tribal development minister Ashok Uike and department officials about the condition of Adivasi residential schools. It is alleged that 584 students have died in these schools. The crime branch is investigating the matter and statements of more than 40 people have been recorded.
nazar: On one side, those who raise questions about a Dalit student's death are detained; on the other, students demanding an inquiry into the deaths of 584 children in Adivasi schools are also picked up. Both incidents show that when people on the margins demand accountability, the state first tries to remove them. This pattern is now becoming clear in Mumbai.
sawal: Is detention the only answer to a complaint of caste harassment?
ref: Chaityabhoomi
The site of Dr Bhimrao Ambedkar's memorial in Mumbai, where large meetings of Dalit and Ambedkarite movements are held.
photo_note: Symbolic image: students' protest

h: Gram sabha said no, yet NOC for nuclear project
dek: Permission for drilling for Tata Power's proposed nuclear project in Rewa was given despite the gram sabha's opposition. Leader of the opposition Umang Singhar has demanded an inquiry.
body: The row over Tata Power's proposed nuclear project in the Rozhouhi-Sarai Kala area of Madhya Pradesh's Rewa district has deepened. Leader of the opposition Umang Singhar alleged in Bhopal on Monday that a no-objection certificate, or NOC, for drilling was issued despite the gram sabha's disagreement.

According to Singhar, the gram sabha unanimously refused to consent to drilling for the project on 3 September, and the panchayat informed the collector on 5 September. The allegation is that on 23 September NOC number 147/2026 was issued, citing an alleged consent letter of 4 September. Sarpanch Komal Sanjay Singh filed a complaint on 8 October demanding an inquiry and the cancellation of the NOC.

Singhar said more than 1,500 families and over 5,000 people live in the area, including a large number of Adivasi and Scheduled Caste families, small farmers and farm labourers. He said Vimla Kol, an elderly Adivasi woman who was on a water satyagraha against the project, has died.

He demanded that studies on environmental impact, seismic risk, water availability and the effects of radiation be made public. Referring to the central Shanti Act, 2025, he also called for transparency in nuclear projects run by private companies in Katni, Chhindwara and Mandsaur.
nazar: Gram sabha consent in Adivasi areas is not just a paper formality; it is the right of the Adivasi community. When an NOC is issued against its decision while citing that same consent, the question is not about one project but about the whole legal framework. In Rewa, the land, water and lives of 5,000 people are at stake, and this decision should not have been taken without their consent.
sawal: When will the government respect the gram sabha's decision?
ref: Shanti Act, 2025
The central law that allows private companies to set up nuclear power projects.
Gram sabha
The assembly of all adult voters of a village, whose consent is considered necessary for decisions on land and forests in Fifth Schedule areas.
photo_note: Women in a tribal village in Umaria district

h: Rape settlement: Supreme Court asks Tripura
dek: The Supreme Court has issued notice over a provision in Tripura's Jamatia customary law that allows offences like rape to be settled with a fine of up to one lakh rupees.
body: The Supreme Court on Monday issued notice to the state government and the Tripura Tribal Areas Autonomous District Council on a public interest petition against a provision of the Jamatia Customary Law of Tripura, 2017, which is accused of allowing serious offences like rape to be settled with a fine of up to one lakh rupees.

The bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana heard the petition. It was filed by Madhumita Bhattacharya and seeks a declaration that section 143 of the Act is unconstitutional. The petition says the provision puts a direct price on a woman's dignity.

The petition argues that the purpose of the Sixth Schedule was to protect tribal identity, customs and land rights, but this does not give customary institutions the power to override national criminal laws on offences like rape. It says section 143, read with section 164, creates a parallel system for rape.

The petition also alleges that the provision denies tribal women equal protection of the criminal law on the basis of their geography and tribal identity. The court has sought replies from all parties and will hear the matter later. The petition was filed through advocate Shaumendu Mukherjee.
nazar: Allowing any crime to be settled with money in the name of custom sends a message not of safety but of danger to women. Protecting tribal identity and Sixth Schedule rights is necessary, but making rape a one-lakh-rupee deal in their name is not written in any constitution. Tribal women in Tripura must be able to trust that national law applies to them too.
sawal: How long will rape be a bargain in the name of custom?
ref: Sixth Schedule
The part of the Constitution that gives tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram self-government and protection for their customs.
Jamatia
A major tribe of Tripura, whose customs were written into a state law in 2017.
photo_note: Supreme Court, New Delhi

h: TIB demands police chief's accountability over crossfire remark
dek: Transparency International Bangladesh has expressed sharp outrage over the remarks of Bangladesh's inspector general of police that the force would resort to crossfire if needed and with the government's approval.
body: Transparency International Bangladesh, or TIB, has expressed sharp outrage over remarks by Bangladesh's inspector general of police, Mohammad Ali Hussain Fakir, that the police would resort to crossfire if needed to maintain law and order, with the government's approval.

TIB has demanded a formal inquiry into the statement, its withdrawal, a public apology and administrative action against the police chief. The organisation also said he should be removed from the post until accountability is fixed. According to TIB, the statement seems to convey that killing people outside the law is an acceptable way to control crime.

TIB executive director Dr Iftekharuzzaman said no government approval can legitimise the extrajudicial killing of anyone. He said the right to life and personal liberty under articles 31 and 32 of the Constitution cannot be cancelled by executive decisions. He cited cases such as the Sinha killings and the Narayanganj seven murders, in which officers of the police and the Rapid Action Battalion have been convicted.

TIB also expressed concern over police allegations against journalists that they criticised the police because they were not paid. The organisation said that if there are allegations against a journalist, legal action should be taken on the basis of evidence, but putting the entire media under suspicion weakens independent journalism.
nazar: In Bangladesh, crossfire is not just a word; it is the memory of hundreds who never reached a courtroom. The police chief saying that killing outside the law can be justified with government approval is a direct attack on the rule of law. When police in India's neighbourhood say such things, it raises questions about human rights across South Asia.
sawal: Who gave the police the right to sanction crossfire?
ref: Crossfire
The alleged name for police action in which suspects are shot dead and the killing is described as an encounter. It has been at the centre of a major human rights controversy in Bangladesh.

h: Whistleblower's sacking illegal, Rs 3.67 crore damages
dek: A Bengaluru court has awarded Rs 3.67 crore to Naveen Kumar Midha, an employee sacked for reporting financial irregularities.
body: A civil court in Bengaluru has held the sacking of Naveen Kumar Midha, a former employee of Willis Towers Watson India Insurance Brokers, illegal and unfair, and ordered the company to pay him Rs 3.67 crore in damages.

Midha had complained of alleged financial irregularities and unethical practices in the company. He alleged that after he brought up matters such as payments to unlicensed intermediaries, fake vendors and irregularities in the accounts, he was first suspended and then sacked.

The court awarded Rs 3,67,97,082 as special damages under the company's whistleblower protection policy, and fixed Rs 10 lakh separately for mental distress. The amount is to be paid within 30 days of the order. The court also directed the company to give him a new, neutral relieving letter and to remove the adverse records related to the suspension.

Judge Shireen Javed Ansari ordered that a complaint be filed before a magistrate against two senior company officials, Vijaykumar Suri and Cedric Lua, on charges of giving false testimony. Midha was suspended in July 2018 and sacked the day after the suspension was lifted in September.
nazar: If whistleblower protection exists only on paper, who will have the courage to report corruption? This ruling matters because the court turned the company's own policy against it and opened the way for action on false testimony. Job security is weakening in India, and rulings like this give employees the confidence to expose wrongdoing inside.
sawal: Why must reporting wrongdoing come at a price?
ref: Whistleblower policy
A company's written policy to protect an employee who reports wrongdoing inside the company from retaliatory action.

h: The Rangit changed, and the Majhis' lives changed too
dek: Dams on the Rangit river in Sikkim and sand mining have taken away the fishermen's income. The Majhi community now lives between new work and old rituals.
body: The Majhi village on the bank of the Rangit river in Jorethang, Sikkim, is an old settlement of a community counted among the oldest dwellers here. For generations the Majhis have fished in the Rangit and the Rangpo and ferried people across in boats. After concrete bridges were built, the boat work ended, and now their fishing livelihood is under threat.

The dam on the Rangit, begun in 2000, is 25 kilometres upstream of the village, while the Jorethang Loop hydropower project started in 2015 only five kilometres upstream. Machines are pulling balwa, the sand used for construction, and stones out of the river, which keeps the water muddy. Shyam Majhi, 63, says the fish have stopped showing themselves.

Of the 15 Majhi households in Jorethang, only three still fish, among them Kumar and his nephew Rupesh. The licence fee has gone up from 50-60 rupees to 3,600 rupees. Kumar earns about 700 rupees from one fishing trip, and the rent from the ground floor of his house also helps. Earlier the fishermen went to the Teesta, thirty kilometres away, but after the Teesta dam burst in 2023 they have not gone back.

Fishing was not the main work of Majhi women; they sold the fish and prepared rations for the long trips. A 52-year-old woman named Kumari Majhi has been an anganwadi worker for about two decades. Every year at Ladi Puja the Majhis bow to the river and their ancestors, show their nets and donga boats, and set a boat adrift on the water after the ritual. Their identity, too, remains a question. In 1975 the Majhis were placed among the Scheduled Castes, in 2013 they were removed from that list, and the following year they were put in the OBC category. In December 2025 the state government again asked the Centre to include the Majhis in the Scheduled Tribes list.
nazar: Dams and sand mining are called development, but the river and the livelihoods tied to it pay the price. The Majhis' fish, their boats and Ladi Puja all rest on the same river, so saving the river is also saving their culture.

The fight over identity is tied to the same question: whom does the state count as tribal? Putting a community on a caste list in 1975 without telling it, then moving it to OBC, shows how much classification is decided from above.
sawal: If the river is shut, where will the livelihood go?
ref: Majhi community
A fisher and boatman community tied to the Rangit and Rangpo rivers of Sikkim, removed from the Scheduled Castes list in 2013 and placed among the OBCs.
Balwa
Sand dredged from the riverbed and used in construction. Mining it in the Rangit muddies the water.
photo_note: Symbolic image: a village by the river

h: Taki Parab in Kalahandi: a festival of harvest and homecoming
dek: After decades, the Kondh community of Odisha held Taki Parab in its own village for Dharni Penu, the earth mother, and people who had gone far away to work came home too.
body: On a cold January evening in Odisha's Kalahandi district, the sun goes down behind the hills, and just then the sound of the nishan drum carries far. This is the start of Taki Parab, the Kondh community's big post-harvest festival. The Kondh are recorded as a Scheduled Tribe in Odisha. People gather from villages in the Thuamul Rampur and Lanjigarh blocks.

For the Kondh, Dharni Penu, the earth mother, is the greatest deity, the one who gives crops, forest and water. Taki Parab is their way of thanking her. Ajay Naik of Taljhapi village says it is the most popular and biggest festival of the Adivasis of Kalahandi.

Each time the festival is held in a new village. The host village is chosen in the month of Dussehra, and then everyone gathers in January after months of preparation. In Taljhapi the festival has returned after decades. Ajay says Taki Parab usually takes place at an interval of 35-36 years, and this time people from 30-40 villages came.

At Dussehra a female sheep is brought in, and the village people feed it day and night. In the morning the priest takes it to the Dharni Khuti, the sacred post, and sacrifices it. Then processions from more than twenty villages come into the open ground dancing to the beat of drums, carrying traditional axes and decorated bamboo sticks. They walk around the post and return with the blood of the sacrifice as prasad.

The meat is shared out. Many believe that leaving a little meat near the Dharni Khuti of one's own village keeps illness away and brings a good next harvest. Sugarcane, coarse grain, pulses and forest produce are sold at the fair, and in many villages even today grain is bartered for things people need. The festival is also a homecoming. Young men who went as far as Kerala to work as labourers come back.
nazar: Taki Parab is not only ritual; it is also a shared knowledge of caring for land, forest and water. When the young go as far as Kerala to work, festivals like this are what keep their link with the village alive.
The state should see these festivals not just as tourism but as part of the local economy and of managing water, forest and land.
sawal: How long will the people who came back for the festival be able to stay in the village?
ref: Dharni Penu
The earth goddess of the Kondh community, seen as the source of crops, forest and water.
Taki Parab
The Kondh community's post-harvest festival, held in one village at a gap of 35-36 years.
photo_note: Symbolic image: a village fair

h: Children wade the Kiul every day, waiting 15 years for a bridge
dek: In Jamui, Bihar, children from the Santhal settlement of Jathar cross the Kiul river on foot to reach school, and their demand for a bridge has brought only assurances.
body: Jathar village, on the bank of the Kiul in Bihar's Jamui district, is a settlement of about two hundred houses. Half the houses belong to Santhal Adivasis, the rest to the Ravidas community, which is listed as a Scheduled Caste. There is no bridge over the river here. To get to school, children have to walk across the Kiul, where the water reaches from the waist to the chest.

Sarojini Baske is in class nine and wants to be a nurse. Srishti Kujur wants to be a doctor. Both cross the river every day. Srishti keeps dry clothes in her bag. For five years her stepmother, Reshmi Devi, carried her across the river in her arms. About 30 Adivasi children from the village cross the river every day, and 20 to 25 of them study at a missionary school.

The government school building in the village collapsed 15 years ago. The school first ran in a community centre, then it was merged with the school in Kerwatari village, about two kilometres away across a deep ravine. Parents say the old school was not as good as the missionary school.

The river does not block only the way to school. Bringing rations, seeing a doctor, reaching a hospital in illness, all of it means crossing the river. The villagers have been asking for a bridge for fifteen years. They have given petitions to ministers, MLAs and officials; every time they got a promise, not work.

The Upper Kiul dam, or Garhi dam, on the Kiul was begun in 1978 and completed in 2004. The project was meant to irrigate 4,141 acres in three blocks of Jamui, but it displaced 427 families and deepened the riverbed. Villagers say that when the dam gates open the sand is washed away, and the river is now 30 feet deep. Now the villagers are preparing to build a bridge themselves, pooling a contribution of about 10,000 rupees.
nazar: A dam promised irrigation, but for the children of Jathar it only made the river deeper. In such a situation, merging the school is not a matter of convenience; it adds to inequality.
In the state's eyes the Adivasi population is small, so their demands are easily put off. The villagers' decision to build a bridge with their own money is proof of that helplessness.
sawal: If there is no bridge, how can there be a right to school?
ref: Upper Kiul dam
A dam built near Garhi village in Jamui between 1978 and 2004, meant to irrigate 4,141 acres.
Tendu leaf
A leaf gathered from the forest and used to make bidis; it is a support for the seasonal income of villages.
photo_note: Symbolic image: villagers crossing a river

h: A kidney sold, then a farmer trapped in a Laos scam den
dek: Roshan Kule, a farmer from Chandrapur, sold a kidney to clear his debt, then fell for a job offer and got trapped in a scam compound in Laos.
body: Roshan Sadashiv Kule of Minthur village in Chandrapur district is a farmer who works in the milk trade. His debt to banks and moneylenders crossed 10 lakh rupees, his house was mortgaged to four finance companies, and a moneylender took the farmland bought with his father's savings. His father's pension, his wife's anganwadi salary and his brother's wages were not enough.

In October 2024 Roshan went to Cambodia and sold his left kidney to clear the debt. Even so, six moneylenders kept hounding him. In February 2025 a friend called, a man who had himself sold a kidney in Cambodia. He dangled a computer operator's job in Laos, 90,000 to one lakh rupees a month, and said the company would pay the expenses.

In June 2025 Roshan and his friend Vishal, who had also sold a kidney, reached Bokeo in Laos, where an agent called Fidee took their passports. The next morning, inside a closed compound among the hills, there were tall buildings and hundreds of young people sitting at computers with 10 to 15 mobile phones each. Roshan says the work was to make fake identities and use AI to cheat people, and to carry out banking fraud. The work was 12 to 14 hours a day, six days a week. The salary was paid, but there was no freedom to go home.

Roshan begged Fidee to let his friend Vishal go, and promised to pay in instalments from his salary to get the passport back. Only then could Vishal return home. Roshan phoned Vijay Wadettiwar, the Leader of the Opposition in the Maharashtra Assembly. With his help, the Indian embassy in Laos and local police got Roshan freed two days later. By the time he got home, the debt had crossed 50 lakh rupees. After his wife attempted suicide and a local YouTube channel reported the story, the police registered an FIR and the state government gave five lakh rupees in help.
nazar: A farmer's debt is not just a bank account. It becomes a stairway that leads to selling a kidney and to a scam den in another country. As long as farming cannot sustain a life, such traps will keep spreading.
Roshan got government help, but there are thousands who have neither a Vijay Wadettiwar nor a channel. Agents who recruit workers need to be watched closely.
sawal: Whom does the weight of debt turn into a labourer?
ref: Golden Triangle
The area along the Myanmar, Laos and Thailand border, where the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone at Bokeo is located.
Kidney racket
The illegal trade of buying kidneys from poor people in debt and selling them to wealthy patients.
photo_note: Symbolic image: a farmer ploughing a field

h: South Pacific youth in the court of climate justice
dek: Law students from the South Pacific knocked on the door of the International Court of Justice, asking industrial countries to pay for climate damage.
body: This is a 52-minute DW Documentary film, written and directed by Felix Golenko. It was released on YouTube on 14 October 2026, and first broadcast on Arte on 29 September 2026. The film follows the campaign of 27 law students who took their demand that industrial countries pay for climate damage to the International Court of Justice.

The students are from the University of the South Pacific and come from islands that will be the first to become unlivable because of rising seas and stronger storms. According to the film's description, these students started the campaign and joined hands with island countries. The case reached the International Court of Justice at the Peace Palace in The Hague, where hearings were held in December 2024.

At the centre of the film are Vishal from Fiji and Jule from Germany. Both work for climate justice and for compensation for the losses suffered by developing countries. With them are the Vanuatu lawyers Anne-Sophie and Lee-Anne, who strengthen the side of the small island states. The film shows them not only in court but also in everyday life and in unequal conditions.

The aim of the case is for the International Court of Justice to hold industrial countries responsible for climate change and to open the way for heavy compensation to the Global South. The United States and Germany argue that international climate law does not clearly make countries responsible for their past emissions. Oil companies, too, want to avoid paying billions in compensation. The film shows how diplomats and lobbyists of big countries try to influence the small island states.

In 2023 the students' campaign won support in the UN General Assembly, and a resolution demanding climate action was passed. The film explains the background of the case through interviews with judges and old footage. In July 2025 the International Court of Justice gave its advisory opinion.

The film connects the language of climate negotiations to the lives of people on the ground. Rising seawater is not just a number for islands where homes and fields are at risk of drowning. The film also shows that the fight for compensation is fought not only in court but in diplomatic corridors too.
nazar: An advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice is not legally binding, but it carries great weight in the politics of climate justice. If responsibility for historical emissions is fixed, the debate over compensation will change not only for island countries but for countries like India too.

But the court's decision will matter only when rich countries turn it into political responsibility. This fight by young people shows that the climate crisis is no distant story; it is a question of someone's home, field and the very existence of a country.
sawal: Who will pay the climate debt?
ref: International Court of Justice (ICJ)
The main judicial body of the United Nations, based in The Hague, which settles disputes between countries and gives advisory opinions.
Advisory opinion
An opinion given by the ICJ at the request of UN bodies. It is not legally binding but carries political weight.
photo_note: A scene from the film

h: The love that survives in Shamsher's silence
dek: Dr. Arundhati's essay suggests reading Shamsher Bahadur Singh's love poems beyond their surrealist images.
body: This essay by Dr. Arundhati, published in Sammukh on 26 October, is about the love poems of Shamsher Bahadur Singh. The writer argues that Shamsher has so far been read as a poet of complex images and abstract feeling, while the real centre of his poetry is love and its incompleteness.

She says this love is made of the suppressed desires of the Indian middle class. It is incomplete and one-sided, and its pain is never fully spoken. The discussion around 'Tooti Hui Bikhri Hui' (Broken, Scattered) includes readings from Namwar Singh to Savita Singh. An objection is also raised: his sense of beauty has no place for the woman toiling at home or the man doing hard labour. The writer does not hide this objection; she understands it alongside Shamsher's romantic vision.

She looks closely at how the poems are built. Broken images, a sentence left unfinished, a long silence and the empty space left after sadness, all these are marks of a lack of love. The language carries the tradition of the Urdu ghazal, from Mir and Ghalib to Dagh and Jauq, and with it a glimpse of English romantic poetry. The title comes from a sher by Ghalib that looks for some Isa, some healer of sorrow. In Shamsher you do not find that cure; only the wanting of it survives.

With the help of remarks by Muktibodh, Malayaj and Rajesh Joshi, the writer also says that Shamsher did not want to make his personal experience general. He wanted to keep what he lived with its own particularity, and that is the honesty of his poetry.
Rather than imposing a thesis, this essay returns to the poetry itself. In Hindi criticism, work written with such patience on a subject like love is rare.
nazar: Today, when poetry is often read like a slogan, this essay reminds us that Shamsher's silence is political too. Such a close reading of love's incompleteness is rare in Hindi criticism.
sawal: Should the lack of love have a place in poetry?
ref: Shamsher Bahadur Singh
A Hindi poet who lived from 1911 to 1993, known for poems such as 'Tooti Hui Bikhri Hui'. His poetry shows the influence of the Urdu ghazal tradition and of English romantic poetry.
Ibn-e-Mariam
An idiom taken from a sher by Ghalib, meaning someone like Isa, the son of Mary, who can cure sorrow. In Shamsher's poetry it becomes the unreachable wish for release from the pain of love.

h: Aabha chooses her own home in the second innings
dek: Rajni Gupta's new story is about a woman who, between two marriages, wins back her own place and her own home.
body: Rajni Gupta's story 'Doosri Paari' (The Second Innings), published in Sammukh on 25 October, revolves around a woman named Aabha. She is married off very young to Vijay, who lets her neither study nor work. Vijay tears up her books and hides her notes, so Aabha decides to get out of the marriage.

Her brother Anil stands by her and decides not to send her back to her in-laws until she finishes her studies. Aabha comes first in class twelve, studies further and rises to a high post in government service. When Vijay returns and talks of living together again, she refuses flatly.

But loneliness and the watchful eye of society close in on her again. Neighbours point fingers and relatives advise a second marriage. In the meantime comes Alok, a big leader with a standing in the government, a man of grand talk. He wants Aabha's simple ways and her earnings, but soon begins to want control over everything in the house and keeps her tied to him by playing on the fear of illness.

Aabha sees through his moves and tells him plainly that she has a right to the house, because she bought it with her own earnings. Alok makes a scene, then quietly packs up and leaves. At the end Aabha watches birds flying in the sky and feels light after years.

The story's strength is that it does not show a second marriage as a straight road to a woman's freedom. Even after financial independence, loneliness and the fear of what people will say can push a woman towards a bad bargain. Rajni Gupta's direct language, full of dialogue, makes the story sound like the houses around us.
nazar: The story does not say that a second marriage is a woman's liberation. It shows that even after becoming self-reliant, loneliness and the fear of society can push a woman into a weak bargain, and that she herself makes the way out.

Control in the name of the house, the salary and the marriage, these three things are still the story of many middle-class homes. So this story becomes not just one woman's story but the story of that whole structure.
sawal: Is financial freedom a woman's whole freedom?
ref: Rajni Gupta
A contemporary Hindi fiction writer whose novel 'Kishori Ka Aasman' and story collection 'Astachal Ki Dhoop' have been widely discussed. She also writes on women's issues.
Doosri Paari
An idiom from cricket meaning here to start life again after a broken marriage. The story shows that this second innings is not so easy.

h: A letter from Delhi that leaves a question behind
dek: In his letter, Aditya Kumar both loves Delhi and questions the growing violence inside it.
body: This letter by Aditya Kumar, published on Hindwi's 'Bela' on 26 October, is addressed to Delhi. At first it sounds like a talk with an old friend, but it soon becomes clear that it is also a political complaint against the city. The writer says the country's condition has worsened, and because it is the centre, Delhi is affected most.

The letter mentions protests, police brutality and attacks by people not in uniform. The writer asks whether innocent people were ever beaten like this before, and women's clothes torn. He gives the example of the Mahabharata, where the unarmed were not attacked, and says that today the public itself is the target.

Amid this anger the sharpest voice is his mother's. She calls twice a day to tell him not to go to Jantar Mantar. She is afraid her son will be taken into custody and she has neither the money nor the contacts to get him out. This fear makes the letter not just a document of ideas but the everyday worry of a family.

The writer calls Delhi the witness of all the movements that have come out of Jantar Mantar. He asks the city to become as it was, to return to its youth like the harsingar in bloom in October. At the end of the letter he wants to stay very close to Delhi, like a drop of dew on the vast earth.

The letter is worth reading because it writes the news of protests not like a report but like a talk with someone close. Anger and love are kept in the same place, and that is what makes it more than a slogan.
nazar: In this time of police action against protests, the letter is not just political comment; it sets the terms of a personal relationship with the city. The mother's daily phone calls show that the price of dissent often falls on families with no access.
Addressing Delhi like a beloved recalls old city poetry, but here it is not a romantic escape; it becomes the question of whose city it is.
sawal: What can those who love the city ask of it?
ref: Jantar Mantar
Delhi's open protest site, where citizens have raised their demands for decades. In the letter it stands for the city's political memory.
Harsingar
A white-and-orange flower that blooms in October, also called parijat. The writer uses it as a memory of Delhi's older, more open self.

h: A place of my own, found on a solo trip
dek: On her first solo trip, Payal Bhardwaj measures the distance of her own fears and bonds more than the roads to Rishikesh.
body: This memoir by Payal Bhardwaj, published on Hindwi's 'Bela' on 24 October, is an account of her first solo journey. She says that when you travel in the roles of wife and mother, home and duties travel with you, so every trip with the family is decided on other people's terms.

Her family and the people around her see this wish as a whim, but after Holi, in March 2026, she sets off for Rishikesh. Without booking a train or a taxi, she travels by government bus, going on through Meerut. She meets a girl carrying a guitar, and there is a stop at a dhaba for tea and Maggi.

On the bus she talks to a young fellow passenger, who asks in surprise whether she is not afraid to go alone. The conversation brings out that, boy though he is, his family does not let him go alone. From this the writer questions how both women and men are raised. When she takes an auto at night, the fear fed by films and news starts talking inside her, but the driver's ease loosens it.

After reaching her hotel room she writes that she had to cover a far greater distance inside herself than on the roads. Breaking the fears and habits built inside is harder than breaking outside bonds. She accepts that solo travel is no magic and that travelling with family is not bad; it is just that sometimes you need to make a place for yourself.

This memoir is different because it has no glossy advertisement for travel. Fear, hesitation and small encounters are its real material. At the end she talks of going back to Rishikesh after Diwali and asks whether that little space she made inside still remains.
nazar: Travel writing often turns into a tourism advertisement. This memoir also writes about its own fears and prejudices. Amid the social watch that still stands over women's movement, this is a necessary document.
The most valuable thing is that the writer does not try to prove herself brave. She accepts that there was fear, and that setting out with that fear was the journey.
sawal: When is going out alone a necessity, and when is it a choice?
ref: Payal Bhardwaj
A writer on travel, women and society in Hindi, who records her experiences as personal notes.
Conditioning
Habits and fears taught since childhood that we take to be natural. The writer says the hardest distance of a solo trip is breaking this inner bond.
