h: When even friends start to look guilty
dek: Giriraj Kiradoo's new poems record friendship, the sense of an enemy, Delhi's streets and the double standards of Hindi literature all at once.
body: Seven new poems by Giriraj Kiradoo were published in Samalochan on 26 October. They share one temper. Here there is friendship, political suspicion, the Delhi Metro, Gaza, and the tricks of the Hindi literary world too.

In the poem 'Dost' (Friend), two people have been companions for years and have usually agreed, but now both have begun to think of calling the other an accused. This fear is not only of politics; it is of an atmosphere in which every conversation is being accounted for. 'Shatrubodh' (the sense of an enemy) is a satire on that same atmosphere, where newspapers, TV, the university and YouTube all tell you that the search for an enemy in Magadha has become an idea.

In 'Rajiv Chowk Metro' comes a flower seller named Abdullah, whose shop was looted by some frenzied boys. In a dream he sees himself wearing nothing but flowers. In 'Delhi Cantt Railway Station' a late-running train, an accident and the station's old violence come back together. The poet sees the city with both its shine and its rubble.

In 'Rafif Ziadah kya kar rahi hai' (What is Rafif Ziadah doing), the poet remembers the Palestinian poet and admits that amid a genocide he himself can do nothing. In 'Citizen Kamra' the question is put to the comedian Kunal Kamra: how did a citizen become so fearless in this air of flattery? The last poem is sharp about those beloved Hindi writers who kept speaking against state repression but also kept flattering the writers who got that same government's laws passed.

The language of these poems is colloquial, with abuse and sarcasm in places, but without the scream of a slogan. Political poetry often forces agreement; these poems also make you uneasy. That is what makes them a necessary document of our time.
nazar: Giriraj Kiradoo's poems do not raise slogans; they record the atmosphere in which friends begin to suspect each other. 'Shatrubodh' and 'Citizen Kamra' are sharp comments on today's literary and political climate.
In these poems the poet does not spare himself either. The poet looks with equal sharpness at his own inaction and at the flattery of his own circle.
sawal: Poetry can bear witness; can it also save?
ref: Giriraj Kiradoo
A Hindi poet, editor and translator born in 1975, co-founder of the online magazine 'Pratilipi'. His poetry comments sharply on politics, the city and the literary climate.
Rafif Ziadah
A Palestinian poet and human rights speaker, known around the world for 'We Teach Life, Sir'. The poem remembers her condition and his own helplessness amid the ongoing violence in Gaza.

h: Old age, alone in the middle of prosperity
dek: Prabhat Ranjan's review of Tripurari Sharan's novel 'Antim Aashray' (The Last Shelter) tells the story of the unravelling of Bihar's middle class.
body: This review by Prabhat Ranjan, published in Jankipul on 26 October, is of Tripurari Sharan's novel 'Antim Aashray'. The reviewer says he tried to read it many times, but childhood memories would come back and the book would be left unfinished. He read it fully during the leave he got in the days of the Delhi protest.

The novel spans a hundred and twenty-five years, and its centre is the Bihar around Muzaffarpur. This is not a story of old memories of the village. In the name of education, the talent here kept going out, and what was left behind was ageing parents and empty earth. The reviewer calls it a history of Bihar's middle class.

The main woman in the story is Rama Devi, who held a good job in the education department and settled her children. After her husband's death the question arises: what will be the last shelter of a woman who has lived with self-respect? Her daughter Roshni dies of cancer, and a childhood friend, Prem Shankar, a lonely businessman in Calcutta, proposes that they live together. Bihar's society does not give room to such companionship.

In the end Rama Devi and Prem Shankar start a scholarship for poor children and begin living in an old age home. The novel shows this not as a tragedy but in a cool, accepting way. In Melbourne the granddaughter tells an acquaintance that her grandmother is about to turn a hundred and has learnt to use Facebook and email.

Prabhat Ranjan considers the novel's greatest quality to be its avoidance of sentimentality. According to him, the Hindi novel has long carried an idealism in the name of Premchand's tradition, one that avoids class reality. This novel puts that reality before us, and in its living language you can smell both the fragrance and the stench of the surroundings.
nazar: This story of a family spread from a Bihar village to foreign countries becomes the story of the middle class across the country. The loneliness of ageing parents and the question of the old age home belong today not to one state but to the whole society.
The review is itself an example of good reviewing, because it reaches the pain of the book's society without turning praise into sentimentality.
sawal: Who decides where old age finally goes?
ref: Tripurari Sharan
A Hindi novelist from Bihar whose first novel is 'Madhopur Ka Ghar'. 'Antim Aashray' is his new novel, published by Setu Prakashan.
Prabhat Ranjan
A Hindi fiction writer and editor of Jankipul, who writes regularly on contemporary novels and stories.
